mstts:express-as.prosody:
Welcome. I’m so glad you’re here with me.
Have you ever noticed how our closest relationships are always changing—how language, identity, and desire seem to shift right beneath our feet? It’s like nothing stays still for long, and that’s actually where the magic begins.
Together, we’re about to dive into these very questions, inspired by Maggie Nelson’s The Argonauts. Through her honest, searching voice, we'll walk through the complexities of love, queerness, and family, and discover just how much our lives can defy neat little boxes.
What happens when the lines between self and other start to blur? Or when the boundaries of gender, motherhood, and partnership don’t look the way we expected? Nelson takes us on a journey where the act of naming and sharing your own story is both difficult and freeing—sometimes all at once.
As we move together through theory, memoir, philosophy, and confession, we’ll see how transformation—whether in our bodies, our relationships, or even the words we use—can feel both radical and beautifully ordinary.
So, if you’re curious about what it really means to love, to change, and to keep growing, you’re in the right place. Let’s begin this exploration, side by side, and see what new possibilities we might discover.

Chapter 1: Searching for Words to Hold a Life
Have you ever felt like some moments are just... too big for words? Like you’re standing right on the edge of something—love, change, maybe even a little bit of fear—and the words you’d normally reach for just don’t quite fit? They’re too small, too stiff, almost like they’re letting you down when you need them most.
That’s where our story really begins—with someone who’s always loved words, who’s always found comfort in language. But suddenly, those same words feel like both a refuge and a trap.
Picture this: it’s early morning, and someone’s sitting quietly at a kitchen table. There’s a cup of coffee, cooling beside a haphazard pile of books. These aren’t just any books—they’re filled with ideas about gender, desire, and the body. Theories that have shaped the way we talk about who we are, and what it means to love.
But as sunlight creeps through the window, it’s pretty clear: no matter how brilliant those theories are, they can’t quite reach the messiness of real life. The person at this table is in love, and that love? It’s changing everything.
Now, falling in love with someone whose body and identity don’t fit neatly into categories—it brings a wild mix of joy and confusion. There’s excitement in the newness, in all the possibilities opening up. But then comes the frustration: the language we have just doesn’t seem big enough. Most folks want to name things, to pin them down: man, woman, straight, gay, mother, father. But what if none of those labels really fit? What if the truth is way more fluid, a little ambiguous?
That’s the real challenge for anyone whose life doesn’t line up with the stories society tells us. The person at the table remembers all those childhood lessons—what families are supposed to look like, what love is supposed to mean. But now, those old rules feel distant, almost meaningless.
Instead, there’s this urge to invent new ways of speaking. New ways of being.
Sure, the books on the table offer some help. They remind us that identity isn’t fixed. That gender and sexuality aren’t just two boxes to check, but whole spectrums that shift and change. That’s comforting, right? But it also raises even more questions. If everything’s fluid, where do you find something solid to hold onto? If words keep failing, how do you make yourself understood?
Later, out in the city, the person walks with their partner—feeling the weight of other people’s eyes. Sometimes folks are curious. Sometimes confused. And sometimes, there’s just plain hostility. It’s a tough reminder: the world isn’t always kind to people who don’t fit the usual mold. But even then, there’s pride. There’s a quiet kind of defiance in holding hands, in refusing to hide who you are.
Back at home, the conversation goes on. Two people, both carrying their own histories, their own scars and dreams, trying to build something together. They talk about the future—maybe kids, maybe family, maybe just what it means to really care for each other. The words come slowly, sometimes awkward. But they keep reaching for each other.
And that’s when it really sinks in: love isn’t about finding the perfect word. It’s about making room for each other’s uncertainty.
The morning slips by, the coffee goes cold, but the search for words continues. It’s slow, sometimes even painful. But there’s hope in it, too. Because in the end, the struggle to name your life—that’s also the struggle to live it fully, honestly, and without apology.

Chapter 2: Building a Family Beyond Old Rules
Imagine this: two people, completely in love, sitting together in a cozy apartment and dreaming about the future. For some couples, that dream follows a familiar script—marriage, kids, maybe a house with a yard. But what happens when those old rules just don’t fit? When the future you want doesn’t come with a ready-made map, you have to create your own.
Picture these partners talking late into the night about the idea of having a child. For one of them, being a parent has always felt like a calling—a deep desire to experience a new life growing inside. The other partner? Well, they’re not so sure. Their perspective is shaped by different experiences, different worries. So, they talk through it all—biological stuff, how bodies change, the way pregnancy can transform someone, body and soul. They wonder about the risks, the hopes, and all the unpredictable things that come with making such a big decision.
For a lot of people, family is tied to tradition. You’re expected to step into certain roles—mother, father, son, daughter. But in this apartment, those labels don’t quite land. These partners have spent years making their own rules, living beyond the boundaries. They already know something powerful: family can be chosen, and the bonds you create through love can be just as strong as any tied by blood.
As the months go by, their decision to have a child starts to feel more real. There are doctor’s visits, honest talks with friends and family, moments of pure excitement—and moments of real doubt. It’s not an easy process. There are endless forms to fill out, complicated questions to answer, and sometimes even harsh judgments to face. Some people cheer them on, others don’t quite get it, and a few are downright unkind. But through all of that, the partners hold tight to each other, determined to build the family they want, not the one others expect.
Pregnancy itself is a wild ride. The body changes in ways that are both magical and strange. Some days, the future feels bright—full of hope and possibility. Other days, fear creeps in, and everything seems uncertain. The real strength comes from leaning on each other, sharing both worries and dreams. That’s when they discover something important: family isn’t just about biology. It’s about caring for each other, showing up, day after day.
And then, the baby arrives. Suddenly, the apartment is alive with new sounds, new routines, and a thousand tiny responsibilities. Sleep becomes a luxury, patience gets tested, but there’s also this incredible sense of wonder. The partners watch their child grow, learning together how to care for this new life. They make mistakes—of course they do—but they never stop trying, never stop caring.
Outside their home, the world still expects families to fit a certain mold. There are forms with boxes that don’t quite match their reality, strangers who ask awkward questions, and systems that just don’t get it. But inside, they create their own rituals and traditions. They teach their child that love is what matters most, that family is something you build, not something you’re simply handed.
Over time, it becomes clear—the old rules just aren’t enough. Family isn’t about squeezing into someone else’s idea of normal. It’s about building a life that feels true, about caring for each other in ways that matter. These partners know their family is different, and yes, sometimes that’s hard. But they also know it’s real, and that’s what makes it enough.

Chapter 3: Living in the Space Between Genders
You know, some folks move through life feeling certain about who they are, almost like they were handed a map at birth. But for others, things aren’t so clear-cut. They find themselves in this in-between space, where the usual categories just don’t really fit.
This chapter is about what it’s like to live in that in-between—about learning to embrace ambiguity instead of running from it.
One partner in this story always felt out of place in their own body. Growing up, they were told how to act, what clothes to wear, even how to move. But none of it ever felt right. There was always this feeling of being watched, of being judged for just not fitting in. So over time, they learned to hide—to play along—but that discomfort? It never really went away.
As an adult, the question of gender gets harder to ignore. There are days when looking in the mirror feels like staring at a stranger. The body can feel like a costume you can’t take off. But then, there are these moments of clarity, when it becomes obvious that gender isn’t just either-or. It’s more like a spectrum—a landscape always shifting, never pinned down by just two points.
Deciding to transition isn’t something you do on a whim. It comes after years of thinking, talking with friends, reading, dreaming. There’s fear—of how people will react, of what might change, of what could be lost. But there’s also hope. The hope that maybe, just maybe, you’ll finally feel at home in your own skin.
Transitioning has its own set of challenges. There are medical appointments, awkward questions from strangers, and moments of real doubt. Some people are supportive, others are confused, and yes, some are even hostile. The body changes in ways that are both exciting and, honestly, a little unsettling. There are days filled with joy, when the future feels bright and open, and days of grief, when it all just feels too heavy.
And through it all, the relationship between these partners grows deeper. They have to talk about things most couples never even think about. They figure out how to support each other, making space for each other’s hopes and fears. They learn that real love isn’t about finding someone who fits a perfect mold—it’s about growing together, about making room for change.
Living in the space between genders means facing constant questions. Strangers want to know: Are you a man or a woman? Which box do you check? But you learn to resist those questions, and to insist on your right to be undefined. That’s when you realize—ambiguity isn’t a weakness. It’s actually a source of strength. Sure, most people are uncomfortable with uncertainty, but for folks living in the in-between, it’s just a way of life.
And over time, there’s a new kind of peace. The body keeps changing, the world keeps challenging, but there’s a feeling of being more fully yourself. The relationship grows stronger, rooted in honesty and real care. These partners know their story doesn’t fit the usual script—but they also know they’re living fully, bravely, and with no apologies.

Chapter 4: The Power and Limits of Language
You know, language is meant to help us connect—to help us really understand each other. But have you ever noticed how sometimes, the words we have just aren’t big enough for the lives we’re living? Especially for people whose experiences don’t fit the usual boxes. Folks who live at the edges, whose ways of loving or being don’t have neat labels—sometimes, the right words just... don’t exist.
In the early days of their relationship, our two partners find themselves stumbling over language. They talk about gender, about desire, about what it truly means to be together. But when it comes time to name their connection—boyfriend, girlfriend, husband, wife—none of those labels feel right. They feel borrowed, awkward, almost like they’re trying on someone else’s clothes.
So, they keep searching. Trying out different words, hoping something will finally feel true. But every term falls just a little bit short.
And it’s not just a personal struggle. It’s political, too. Our world loves categories—it’s built on the idea that everyone can be sorted into tidy little boxes. But for the people who don’t fit? Language becomes a battleground. Every word is a negotiation, a way of saying, “Hey, I deserve to exist on my own terms.”
The partners start reading, talking to friends, going to events—trying to figure it all out. And they discover something important: language is alive. It’s always shifting, always evolving. People invent new words, reclaim old ones. But even the best words can only stretch so far. There are always going to be gaps—things that just can’t be said.
Sometimes, when the words run out, the partners find comfort in silence. They learn to talk in other ways—maybe it’s a touch, a look, or just sharing a laugh. They realize that real intimacy isn’t just about what you say, but about being present, about being okay with the unknown. Most people want clear answers, want everything spelled out. But these two? They learn that not knowing is okay, too.
As their family grows, the dance with language gets even trickier. There are forms to fill out, questions from doctors and teachers, and chats with other parents. They have to decide, every time, how to describe themselves and their family. Sometimes, it’s just easier to go with the simplest answer, just to avoid a hassle. But other times, they stand their ground—even when it’s tough.
Over time, it becomes clear: language is both a tool and a trap. Sure, it helps us find each other, build community, make sense of our lives. But it can also limit, exclude, or even erase people’s experiences. The partners learn to use language carefully, and to be honest about what it can and can’t do. They know words will never be enough. But they also know that silence isn’t an option.

Chapter Five: Love, Change, and the Courage to Be Seen.
You know, we often picture love as this steady, unchanging thing—a safe harbor in the middle of a storm. But for these partners, love isn’t just a place to hide from the world. It’s a force that transforms them, that asks for courage, and, maybe hardest of all, asks them to risk being truly seen.
At first, love feels simple. There’s excitement, laughter, the rush of discovering each other. Everything seems easy. But as their relationship grows deeper, new challenges start to show up. Suddenly, they’re learning how to care for each other through all kinds of change—pregnancy, transition, and the daily struggles of building a life side by side.
Of course, there are moments of doubt. Times when everything just feels too hard. Maybe one partner worries about losing themselves, afraid of what’ll happen if things change too much. The other might fear being left behind, scared that their own needs are just too much. Yet, through all of it, they keep choosing each other. Over and over, they show up, especially when it’s tough.
What they discover is that love isn’t really about finding someone who never changes. It’s about finding ways to change together—to make space for each other’s growth. They learn that intimacy isn’t about knowing every little thing, but about being open to learning, to being surprised, and to allowing themselves to be vulnerable.
And that takes real courage. Because being seen—really seen—can be uncomfortable. It means owning up to fears, asking for help, trusting that your partner will stay even when you’re at your most unsure. Most of us are scared of change, scared of losing control. But they realize that change isn’t the enemy. In fact, it’s what makes their love real.
As their family grows, new challenges come up. There are sleepless nights, endless chores, and plenty of moments when frustrations boil over. But there are also moments of pure joy—watching their child take a first step, sharing a quiet morning together, and slowly building a life that’s all their own.
Over time, it becomes clear: love isn’t about perfection. It’s about persistence—the willingness to keep trying, even when things get messy. These partners know their lives won’t ever fit the usual script. But they also know they’re creating something real, something that lasts.

Chapter Six: Theory Meets the Mess of Real Life
You know, there’s a certain comfort in theory. It gives us this promise of order—a way to bring sense to all the chaos swirling around us.
But what happens when all those tidy ideas smack right into the everyday messiness of real life? Well, things rarely go the way we imagined.
Picture this: it’s late afternoon, and one partner is curled up with a book. They’re reading about the fluidity of identity, how gender is something we construct, not something fixed. The words are beautiful, and the arguments make perfect sense.
But then—the baby starts crying in the next room. The other partner is fumbling with a bottle, trying to calm things down. And suddenly, the gap between theory and practice feels enormous.
It’s easy to talk about queerness, about pushing back against norms, when you’re in a cozy classroom or chatting over coffee. But try filling out paperwork at the pediatrician’s office, or explaining to a neighbor why your family looks a little different. It’s a whole different story.
These partners end up caught right in the middle—torn between the world of big ideas and the world of diapers, bills, and sleepless nights.
Sometimes, the theories are a lifeline. They help explain why things can feel so tough, why the world is so determined to sort everyone into neat little boxes.
Other times? Those same theories feel far away, almost out of reach.
One morning, after a particularly rough start to the day, the partners meet up with a friend for coffee. This friend gets it—they live in the world of theory, too. The partners vent about endless forms and awkward questions, and the friend just listens, nodding along.
Then, the friend grins and says, Theory is great... but it doesn’t change diapers.
The partners laugh, and for a moment, some of that heaviness lifts.
That’s when it really sinks in—living outside the norm means you’re always balancing ideals with the reality right in front of you. Most people never have to think about this; their lives fit the scripts they’ve been given. But for these partners, every single day is a balancing act.
They figure out how to hold onto the insights that matter, and let go of the rest.
They learn it’s possible to honor all the messiness of real life—without giving up hope for something better.
With time, the partners find a rhythm. They use theory as a tool, not a rulebook. They start trusting their own instincts, making choices that feel right for their family—even if those choices don’t fit anyone else’s definition of “normal.”
Sure, that gap between theory and practice never really disappears. But it gets less intimidating. In fact, it turns into a space for creativity, for invention—a place to build a life that’s both thoughtful and wonderfully real.

Chapter 7: Parenting at the Edge of the Map
Let’s be honest—parenthood is usually called a journey, but for these partners, it’s more like stepping into the wild, with no map in sight. They're building a family that doesn’t come with instructions or easy answers. Every day brings something new—a question, a challenge, and, of course, moments of pure joy.
In those early months, everything’s a blur. Feedings, naps, and the never-ending laundry pile. The partners trade off holding their tiny child, noticing every little detail—the delicate fingers, the very first smiles. There’s so much wonder in those moments, but there’s also this quiet thread of anxiety running underneath. Will their child be safe out there? Will they be accepted for who they are? How do you even begin to explain a family like theirs to a world that still likes to put everything in neat little boxes?
As their child gets older, the questions change, but they don’t get any easier. On the playground, other parents ask, “Where’s mommy?” or “Who’s daddy?” And at school, those forms still demand to know who the “real” parent is. The partners do their best—they answer patiently on some days, and with a bit of frustration on others. They watch their child wrestle with these questions too—sometimes confused, sometimes standing tall with pride.
Then, one afternoon, their child comes home from school holding a drawing. It’s messy, bursting with colors and wild lines. You see two adults, a child, and a whole jumble of hearts. Looking at that picture, the partners are overwhelmed with emotion—pride, love, and this fierce determination to protect the beautiful world their child imagines.
Parenting at the edge of the map means you’re always improvising. You teach your child to be brave, to be kind, and to trust that their family is real and worthy—even if others don’t see it yet. You start to find your people in unexpected places—other families that don’t fit the mold, friends who show up when you need them, strangers who offer a warm smile instead of a cold stare.
Sure, there are hard days. Sometimes, the weight of being different feels like too much to carry. But there are also these little, unexpected joys—a neighbor who drops by with cookies, a teacher who asks, “How can I support your child best?” Or a friend who just listens, without judgment.
Over time, the partners realize they’re not as alone as they once thought. There are others out there, too—people building families on the edge of the map, lighting the way for those who will follow.

Chapter 8: The Body as a Site of Change
You know, we’re told that our bodies should tell the truth about who we are. That’s what most people think, right? But for these partners, the body isn’t just a reflection—it's a place where identity, desire, and history are always in motion, sometimes colliding, sometimes blending in unexpected ways.
Picture one partner, right in the middle of transition. Their body is changing—sometimes it’s thrilling, like finally coming home to yourself. Other days, though, it can feel strange or unfamiliar, almost like looking in the mirror and seeing someone else. Clothes start to fit differently, voices deepen or lighten, and even simple things—like walking down the street—feel charged with new meaning. There’s a constant awareness, a mix of excitement and caution, because every encounter could bring connection… or risk.
The other partner, having gone through pregnancy and birth, knows transformation too. Their body carries marks—scars, stretch lines, aches that linger. There’s pride in what their body’s accomplished, but also a quiet sense of loss. The body feels changed, sometimes like it doesn’t quite belong to them anymore.
Together, these partners talk about these changes. Sometimes they laugh about it, sometimes it’s raw and emotional. They figure out new ways to touch, to connect, to find comfort and intimacy when things feel uncertain.
Most people don’t really think about their bodies day to day. They assume everything about gender and identity is obvious, written right there in flesh. But for these two, the body isn’t an answer—it’s a question. It’s not fixed, not destiny. Instead, it’s a space for possibility, for change, for becoming something new.
And over time, they start to honor that. They find doctors who really listen, friends who truly get it, and communities where difference is celebrated, not hidden. They discover that the body’s changes aren’t something to fear—they’re a sign that life is always moving, always becoming. And maybe, just maybe, that’s where the real truth lives.

Chapter 9: Making Home in a World That Resists.
When we think about home, most of us picture a place where we can finally breathe—a place that feels safe, where the outside world can’t reach us. But for these partners, finding home is about so much more than just signing a lease or moving into a new apartment. It’s about building a space where they’re free to be themselves, and where their family can actually thrive, without having to look over their shoulders.
But let’s be honest—it’s not always a smooth journey. Sometimes, the search for home means running into landlords who see their family and hesitate, or neighbors who can’t help but stare. There are systems out there that just don’t know what to make of a family like theirs. Navigating all this? It takes grit. Sometimes patience wins the day, and other times, it’s anger that pushes them forward.
So, what do they do? They take the place they’ve got and make it theirs. They paint the walls in colors that bring them joy, plant gardens out front, and hang up pictures that tell their story—reminders of where they’ve come from and who they are at their core.
But it’s inside their home where the real magic happens. They build rituals—maybe it’s Sunday pancakes, sharing bedtime stories, or just enjoying quiet evenings together on the couch. These little moments? They become anchors, steady points in a world that can feel anything but welcoming. By inviting friends in and building community, they make space for others who don’t always fit the usual mold.
Still, the world outside is never too far away. There are protests on the news, laws that threaten families just like theirs, and stories that break your heart. The partners don’t hide this from their child—they talk honestly, trying to explain without giving in to despair. They teach their child to stand tall, to be proud, and to know—deep down—that their family is absolutely real and deserving of respect.
In the end, making home becomes an act of resistance—a way of saying, “We matter. Our love creates a safe place, even when everything feels uncertain.” Over time, they discover something powerful: home isn’t just a place you live. It’s something you do, every single day. It’s about caring for each other, telling the truth, and holding onto hope, no matter what the world throws at you.

Chapter 10: The Ongoing Work of Becoming
You know, it's easy to imagine that one day, everything in life will just... settle down. That all our big questions will finally get answered, the tough parts will smooth out, and the family will feel complete. But for these partners, life doesn’t really work that way. It’s this ongoing process—always shifting, always becoming something new. There’s always another challenge, another joy, another way to grow together.
As their child gets older, new questions keep popping up. Like, how do you talk about what makes us different in a way that feels empowering, not shameful? Or, how do you truly support each other through all the changes—through the grief, and even those everyday disappointments that sneak up on us? And maybe the biggest one: how do you keep loving, keep hoping, keep building something beautiful, even when the world seems set on holding you back?
There aren’t any simple answers here. Some days, these partners feel strong—like they can take on anything together. Other days? They’re tired. Maybe a little uncertain, maybe even afraid. But no matter what, they keep showing up. For themselves, for each other, for their child. That’s where they discover something powerful: becoming isn’t really about reaching a destination. It’s a way of living. It’s about staying open, being willing to keep trying, and—most of all—choosing to keep loving.
When the partners look back on everything—the risks they took, the losses they faced, the moments that made their hearts soar—they can see how far they’ve come. How much they’ve truly grown. And sure, the work isn’t ever really finished. There will always be another challenge, another possibility waiting ahead. But here’s the thing—they know they’re not alone. There are others out there, too, building their lives from the edges, standing up for the right to exist, to love, to become.

As we wrap up, let's take a moment to really sit with what this journey has shown us. Living outside the lines isn't just a single act of bravery, is it? It's something you choose, every single day. The Argonauts reminds us of people who won't let other folks define them, who create family and home even when life feels uncertain, and who learn that love isn’t about squeezing into someone else’s shape—it's about making room for each other to grow. Here are a few gentle reminders to carry with you: Language? It's just a tool—it can’t possibly capture every truth you live. Family isn’t about following someone else’s script; it’s built through care, day by day. Your body is always changing, never a final answer or a fixed destiny. And while theory might point the way, life itself is always a little messier—and honestly, even more beautiful. Becoming yourself? That’s never finished. There’s no finish line—just the next step forward. If you ever find yourself searching for words, or for a sense of home, or just hoping to be seen—remember, you’re not on your own. The world won’t always make it easy, but there’s real power in the questions you ask and the life you build, moment by moment. Let yourself be changed by love, by uncertainty, by the simple act of showing up every day. Trust that your story matters, even if it doesn’t fit the usual patterns. And above all—know that courage isn’t about “arriving.” It’s about keeping on, together, with hope, honesty, and care. Here’s to the ongoing, beautiful work of becoming—one step at a time.
